## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/02.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Background
Concepts and Terminology</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/03.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">COVID-19 Pandemic
• The COVID-19 Pandemic led to the largest disruption of education in the
history of the United States.
• Three years into the pandemic the impacts are still being felt by students:
academically, emotionally, physically, and financially and educators.
• In this presentation, we address three things:
1. Academic Impact: What is it and what happened to students in
Hawaii?
2. Academic Recovery: What is it and what is happening to students in
Hawaii currently?
3. Now What?: How can impact and recovery data be leveraged to help
students going forward? Evidence-based investigations of what is
working.</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/04.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">What is Academic Impact?
• Academic Impact: Also referred to as learning loss or unfinished
learning.
• The pandemic and all its ensuing disruptions functioned as an
“academic headwind”, impeding the academic progress (i.e.,
learning) of students.
• Headwinds impede progress in two ways:
▪ They slow one’s rate of progress (speedometer)
▪ And by slowing one’s rate of progress they lead to less distance being travelled
(odometer).
• Academic impact decreases the rate of student learning
(deceleration) which, in turn, leads to lower attainment.</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/05.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">What is Academic Recovery?
• Academic Recovery: Also referred to as learning recovery
• Academic recovery refers to increases in student learning
sufficient to ameliorate previous academic impacts.
• Academic recovery is analogous to a tailwind, increasing the
rate of student learning (acceleration) which, in turn leads to
higher attainment.
• To understand whether academic recovery is occurring, one
must know the extent of academic impact.</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/06.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Impact &amp; Recovery: Educational Assessment
• Hawaii’s Smarter Balanced and WIDA-ACCESS are ideally
suited to help investigate academic impact and recovery.
• With educational assessments, impact/recovery manifest as:
• Decrease/increase in student growth
• Decrease/increase in velocity = deceleration/acceleration
• Decreases/increases in student growth lead to decreases/
increases in student attainment
• Growth is to speedometer as attainment is to odometer.</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/07.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Impact &amp; Recovery: Educational Assessment
• Two time frames:
• Impact: Spring 2020 through Summer 2021
• Recovery: Fall 2021 through Summer 2022
• Two assessments:
• Smarter Balanced Assessment Data (ELA &amp; Mathematics)
• Impact: Spring 2019 to Spring 2021 (Testing cancelled in 2020)
• Recovery: Spring 2021 to Spring 2022
• WIDA-ACCESS English Language Proficiency Data
• Impact: Winter 2020 to Winter 2021
• Recovery: Winter 2021 to Winter 2022
• Two methods:
• Attainment: Change in student attainment (odometer)
• Growth: Change in student growth (speedometer)</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/09.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Impact Phase
• During spring 2019-2020 and the 2020-2021 academic year, school was extremely
disrupted due to pandemic related mitigation efforts.
• Due to all the disruptions the expectation was that student learning would be
impacted (i.e., would slow down) leading to lower student growth and lower
student attainment.
• Data from two sources was utilized to examine the extent to which the pandemic
impacted student learning:
• Smarter Balanced data from 2019 and 2021
• WIDA-ACCESS data from 2020 and 2021</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/10.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Academic Impact
•Using student attainment and growth, academic
impact is categorized along a continuum ranging
from severe to modest to none.
•Academic impact is examined both overall and
by academic quintile.
•Academic impact was examined by each grade
and content area tested for all students as well
as for several demographic subgroups.
•Non-participation in 2021 assessments was
larger than normal. We utilized multiple
imputation techniques to understand the extent
to which missing data impacted observed
results.</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/16.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Recovery Phase
• During the 2021-2022 academic year, school returned to normal for most
students.
• The hope was that a return to normal would lead recovery of the academic losses
incurred by students.
• Because learning slowed during the initial phase of the pandemic, to make up for
those losses, learning must accelerate to rates above normal in order to catch-up
for those loses.
• Data from two sources was utilized to examine whether recovery is occurring:
• Smarter Balanced data from 2021 and 2022
• WIDA-ACCESS data from 2021 and 2022</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/17.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Academic Recovery
•Using student attainment and growth,
academic recovery is categorized along a
continuum ranging from deterioration to
recovery.
•Academic impact is examined both overall
and by academic quintile.
•Academic impact was examined by each
grade and content area tested for all students
as well as for several demographic subgroups.</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/19.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Overall Recovery
• Analysis of 2022 SBA and ACCESS data indicates a lot of trends in Hawaii to be
happy about.
• In both ELA and mathematics, learning acceleration was at least as much to be
considered stabilization and in many cases could be considered as genuine
recovery.
• Compared to a dozen other states that the Center conducts these analyses, Hawaii
comes out as the best in terms of pandemic recovery.
• Results from 2023 data will be critical to assess whether these exemplary rates of
learning (beyond what the state experience pre-COVID) are being maintained.</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/20.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Now What
Leveraging Assessment Data to Help Students Overcome COVID-19 Academic Impacts</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/21.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Exemplar Schools: Impact &amp; Recovery
• Original discussions about examining ROI were refined to examine Return on Activities:
• Identify outlier schools in terms of impact/recovery.
• Investigate whether activities (or lack thereof) could potentially be responsible for the
school’s outlier status.
• For schools with plausible activities leading to exemplary recovery, investigate links to
relevant investment/funding.
• Step 1 is to find these outlier schools.
• We investigated schools along two dimensions:
• Academic Impact (2019 to 2021 decrease in student learning)
• Academic Recovery (2021 to 2022 increase in student learning relative to pre-
pandemic 2018-2019 learning)</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/22.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Exemplar Schools: Impact &amp; Recovery
• We searched for exemplar schools to place into three categories
• Large Impact/Large Recovery (9 schools)
• Minimal Impact/Large Recovery (4 schools)
• Large Impact/Poor Recovery (3 schools)
• 16 schools were sampled across a diverse range of socio-economic and
demographic characteristics with the goal of finding replicable strategies that can
be used by Hawaii schools to help students recover.</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/23.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Exemplar Schools: Impact &amp; Recovery
• Some initial findings:
• Distributive leadership works well in “normal” situations, authoritative leadership is
necessary during a crisis.
• Everyone was in crisis mode from March 2020-August 2020
• Strong leadership adapted existing / implemented new programs quickly and
effectively
• Funding was not a benefit or limitation for recovery
• Strong leadership went into the community, school funds, foundations – found the
money when needed or paid out of their own pocket for food distribution, providing
masks, providing other health services
• Strong leadership focused on the whole school community including parents and staff
• Data use for identifying struggling students was flexible</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Status Impact

Black Line: 2019 (pre-covid) scaled-score
distribution.

The impact of the pandemic on student
achievement (decrease) is illustrated as the area
between the black line (top) and red line
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/35.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Baseline SGP: What is Recovery

• Given the negative pandemic impacts, any recovery implies learning acceleration.
• However, not all acceleration can be considered recovery
• Acceleration versus 2021 versus acceleration versus 2019
V-Shaped Recovery (&gt; 60)
60 U-Shaped Recovery (50 to 60)

Median 2021 Baseline SGP 50 Median 2022 Baseline SGP
L-Shaped “Recovery” (40 to 50)

Downward Spiral (&lt; 40) Note: Any median SGP above 30
in 2022 would be considered
acceleration. But only values
10 above 50 would be sufficient to
begin catching students up to
where they would have been
absent the pandemic.</div>
```
